name: FOMO Drives Bad QC Decisions
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Fear of Missing Out Is Not an Investment Thesis
lesson.summary: Fear of missing out, the anxiety that everyone else is capturing gains you will be shut out of, systematically overrides the careful probability weighing that ethical investment duty demands, making it one of the most reliable ways a systemic hype cycle produces irrational individual decisions.
lesson.body:
FOMO in QC investment names a specific, recognizable pattern: investors, institutions, or individual researchers piling into quantum computing opportunities primarily because they fear being left behind, often triggered by media coverage of a competitor's funding round, a geopolitical announcement, or a widely shared claim of a technical milestone. Ethical investment duty, covered two chapters back, is the obligation to reason from real, disclosed probability rather than from narrative or social pressure. FOMO is worth studying specifically because it is one of the main psychological forces that makes people, including people who genuinely know better, quietly abandon that obligation.

The underlying mechanism is well understood in behavioral terms. FOMO exploits loss aversion, the well documented tendency for the pain of a loss to be felt more sharply than the pleasure of an equivalent gain, but with a twist: watching a peer or a competitor appear to gain from a trend you chose to sit out often feels like a distinct and separate kind of loss, on top of whatever the numbers actually show. That extra emotional weight pushes people toward action, buying into a fund, committing a lab to a new direction, joining a company, even in situations where a calm, probability of success based assessment would not support the decision.

FOMO does not operate only on individuals in isolation. It is manufactured, often without any deliberate intent, by the same systemic loops covered earlier in this book, at every level of the system. The geopolitical arms race loop manufactures FOMO at the national level, through reasoning like if we do not fund this aggressively, a rival nation will get there first. The sunk cost escalation loop manufactures it at the institutional level, through reasoning like everyone else here is already committed, so we cannot be the ones who pull back now. The hype reinforcement loop manufactures it at the individual retail investor level, through media coverage that makes other people's apparent gains highly visible while making the much larger number of quiet losses much less visible. In each case, FOMO is doing structurally the same job: converting a systemic pressure into an individual decision that bypasses careful evaluation.

This is exactly why ethical investment duty and fiduciary responsibility matter more, not less, during a hype cycle, precisely because FOMO tends to be strongest exactly when calibrated judgment is scarcest. A useful concrete check comes from noticing the mechanism in yourself: a financial advisor who feels their own version of FOMO, worrying that clients will leave if they are not given access to the latest quantum play, is experiencing the identical psychological mechanism as the client they are advising. Recognizing that shared vulnerability, rather than assuming professionals are somehow immune to it, is often the first real step toward resisting it.
